Bounds for the absolute accuracy when some profiles are never verified

Source: R/bounds.R
accuracy_bounds.Rd

Gives the range of values that the prevalence and the sensitivity and specificity of each test (or rule) can take, whatever the proportion of diseased subjects in the response profiles that are never verified.

Usage

accuracy_bounds(fit, rules = fit@data@tests, odds_ratio = NULL, level = 0.95)

Arguments

fit

A model fitted with baysesp() and saturated().

rules

Rules or test names, see rule_accuracy(). By default, the individual tests.

odds_ratio

The odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects with the same response profile, \(\exp(\beta)\): a single positive number (one value only; to compare several values, call the function once for each). 1 means that verification does not depend on the disease status (missing at random); values above 1 mean that the diseased are verified more often. The default, NULL, uses 1 for a model fitted with verification = mar(), and gives an error for a model fitted with verification = mnar(), for which a value must be given.

level

Probability of the credible intervals.

Value

A data frame with columns quantity, lower_bound, upper_bound (posterior medians of the bounds), lower and upper (the lower quantile of the lower bound and the upper quantile of the upper bound).

Details

When some profiles (combinations of test results) are never verified, the data say nothing about how many diseased subjects they contain, and the absolute accuracy depends on it. A prior on that proportion gives a single answer, which rests entirely on the prior (Buzoianu and Kadane, 2008). These bounds instead show what the data alone allow (Gustafson, 2015): the lowest and highest value of each quantity when the proportion of diseased in the never-verified profiles ranges from 0 to 1. They do not depend on the prior. Wide bounds mean that the absolute accuracy is mostly determined by the assumption on the never-verified profiles.

The bounds also depend on the odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects with the same profile, which the data cannot estimate either: they are computed for one fixed value, odds_ratio (by default 1, verification that does not depend on the disease). Call the function again with other values to see how the bounds move.

Bounds. Let \(\psi_t = P(D = 1 \mid T = t)\) be the proportion of diseased in profile \(t\) and \(\omega_t = P(T = t)\) its frequency. For a profile with verified subjects \(\psi_t\) is estimated from the data: with odds ratio of verification \(OR = \exp(\beta)\), \(\psi_t = v_t \phi_t + (1 - v_t)\,\mathrm{expit}(\mathrm{logit}\,\phi_t - \beta)\), where \(v_t\) is the fraction of verified subjects in the profile and \(\phi_t\) the proportion of diseased among them (with \(OR = 1\), \(\psi_t = \phi_t\)). For a never-verified profile \(\psi_t\) is unknown. For a rule \(R\) that declares no never-verified profile positive, let $$A_R = \sum_{t: r_R(t) = 1} \omega_t \psi_t, \qquad B_R = \sum_{t: r_R(t) = 1} \omega_t (1 - \psi_t),$$ the proportions of subjects who are declared positive and are diseased or healthy, \(c\) the proportion of diseased subjects with a verified profile and \(\omega_0\) the frequency of the never-verified profiles. Then \(Se_R = A_R / \pi\) and \(1 - Sp_R = B_R / (1 - \pi)\), and since \(c \le \pi \le c + \omega_0\), $$\frac{A_R}{c + \omega_0} \le Se_R \le \frac{A_R}{c}, \qquad 1 - \frac{B_R}{1 - c - \omega_0} \le Sp_R \le 1 - \frac{B_R}{1 - c}.$$ The upper bound of the sensitivity and the lower bound of the specificity are the values of the naive analysis that considers healthy every subject with a never-verified profile; the other bounds correspond to considering all of them diseased.

The bounds are functions of identified parameters (and of the odds ratio), so they have a posterior distribution: the result gives their posterior medians and a credible region that contains the whole identification interval with probability at least level (Gustafson, 2015). For rules that declare a never-verified profile positive the bounds are NA.

The accuracy is defined for a rule \(R\), which declares a subject positive or negative from the response profile \(t\), the vector of the results of the tests: \(r_R(t) = 1\) if the profile is declared positive, 0 otherwise. A single test is the rule "this test is positive". The quantities depend on the prevalence \(\pi = P(D = 1)\) and on the distribution of the profiles in the diseased, \(\theta_{1,t} = P(T = t \mid D = 1)\), and in the healthy, \(\theta_{0,t} = P(T = t \mid D = 0)\):

  • sensitivity (Se): $$Se_R = P(R \textrm{ positive} \mid D = 1) = \sum_t r_R(t)\, \theta_{1,t},$$ the proportion of diseased subjects that the rule declares positive. It is also called the true positive rate (TPR);

  • specificity (Sp): $$Sp_R = P(R \textrm{ negative} \mid D = 0) = 1 - \sum_t r_R(t)\, \theta_{0,t},$$ the proportion of healthy subjects that the rule declares negative; \(1 - Sp_R\) is the false positive rate (FPR);

  • positive predictive value (PPV): $$PPV_R = P(D = 1 \mid R \textrm{ positive}) = \frac{\pi\, Se_R}{\pi\, Se_R + (1 - \pi)(1 - Sp_R)},$$ the probability that a subject declared positive is diseased;

  • negative predictive value (NPV): $$NPV_R = P(D = 0 \mid R \textrm{ negative}) = \frac{(1 - \pi)\, Sp_R}{(1 - \pi)\, Sp_R + \pi\, (1 - Se_R)},$$ the probability that a subject declared negative is healthy.

Sensitivity and specificity describe the rule and do not depend on the prevalence; the predictive values describe what a result means for a subject, and change with the prevalence of the population. For combined rules, such as any_positive(), the accuracy depends on the joint distribution of the tests, not only on their individual sensitivities and specificities (Torrance-Rynard and Walter, 1997; Vacek, 1985).

Each quantity is computed from every posterior draw of \(\pi\), \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_1\). The results report its posterior mean and median and an equal-tailed credible interval with probability level.

References

Buzoianu, M. and Kadane, J. B. (2008). Adjusting for verification bias in diagnostic test evaluation: A Bayesian approach. Statistics in Medicine, 27(13), 2453–2473. doi:10.1002/sim.3099

Gustafson, P. (2015). Bayesian Inference for Partially Identified Models: Exploring the Limits of Limited Data. Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, FL.

Torrance-Rynard, V. L. and Walter, S. D. (1997). Effects of dependent errors in the assessment of diagnostic test performance. Statistics in Medicine, 16(19), 2157–2175. doi:10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19971015)16:19<2157::AID-SIM653>3.0.CO;2-X

Vacek, P. M. (1985). The effect of conditional dependence on the evaluation of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 41(4), 959–968. doi:10.2307/2530967

See also

accuracy_ratios(), sensitivity_analysis()

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
# profile (0,0) is never verified
d <- simulate_study(n = 2000, prevalence = 0.2,
                    sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.8),
                    specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.95),
                    verification_prob = c(0, 0.9, 0.9, 1))
d <- baysesp_data(d, tests = c("A", "B"), verified = "verified", disease = "disease")
fit <- baysesp(d, saturated(unverified_prevalence_prior = elicit_beta(0.03, 0.06)),
               seed = 1)
accuracy_bounds(fit)
#>     quantity lower_bound upper_bound     lower     upper
#> 1 prevalence   0.1998029   0.8397389 0.1825565 0.8555800
#> 2      Se[A]   0.2150756   0.9045453 0.1958355 0.9325346
#> 3      Sp[A]   0.2154108   0.8429136 0.1716957 0.8601760
#> 4      Se[B]   0.1912372   0.8044312 0.1726520 0.8420550
#> 5      Sp[B]   0.7360968   0.9472660 0.6848990 0.9580449
accuracy_bounds(fit, odds_ratio = 2)
#>     quantity lower_bound upper_bound     lower     upper
#> 1 prevalence   0.1965725   0.8365040 0.1795691 0.8525168
#> 2      Se[A]   0.2132777   0.9082051 0.1941214 0.9353522
#> 3      Sp[A]   0.2174917   0.8408455 0.1741221 0.8579767
#> 4      Se[B]   0.1906394   0.8123313 0.1721827 0.8492972
#> 5      Sp[B]   0.7348246   0.9461930 0.6850631 0.9568404
# }
